title: I Resent Contentment, Even a Raincloud’s Smile
intro: Abu al-Ala' al-Ma'arri mourns his father, Abd Allah ibn Sulayman, in poem 41 of Saqt al-Zand. He resents even the flash that makes a raincloud seem to smile. He follows sandgrouse and wild asses to water, asking what makes life dear even to creatures that suffer for it. When he turns to his father, the sound of a dying man’s breath comes back to him, and even a singer with a flawless voice seems to be mourning.

translation: I resent contentment, even a raincloud’s smile.
May only a scowling sky rain on me.
1.sharh: Lightning lights up a cloud as teeth light up a face. He still wishes for rain, ordinarily a blessing, and stipulates the expression its giver must wear.

translation: If a smile should draw my teeth into view, may my mouth
be the mouth of a wide wound that bleeds without a tooth.
2.sharh: His smile can draw a tooth into the light as a hand draws a sword. A gaping wound has the opening of a smile, but anyone looking at it will see pain.

translation: As though its front teeth were young women
whose good name is guarded by keeping them indoors.
3.sharh: His lips close like the door of a house whose young women are kept from view. The convention of protecting a woman’s reputation gives his resolve to conceal a smile almost the weight of a duty.

translation: The nights have passed judgement on my father.
Death’s spears have always had the power to pierce.
4.sharh: Only now does he name the person whose death has put his own face under such discipline. The nights deliver a sentence on one man, and death wields a weapon it has always possessed.

translation: He went pure in body, soul and sleep,
in waking wishes, collar, hem and cuff.
5.sharh: Character shows even in what he dreamed and what he wished for when awake. The clothes carry the argument from the breast that harbours thoughts down to the hand that might take what belongs to someone else.

translation: I wish I knew whether his gravity will lighten
when Uhud turns to wool at the Resurrection.
6.sharh: When mountains become like tufts of wool at the Resurrection, even the weight of Uhud will be gone. The son measures his father’s gravity against a mountain so that the ordinary sense of weight returns to the word.

translation: Will he hurry with the others to the brimming pool,
or shrink from the press and wait his turn?
7.sharh: At the Prophet’s pool, the thirsty will gather to drink. The son can still picture his father doing a familiar thing even there, stepping aside until others have had their fill.

translation: His judgement made him bolder and more generous.
Some men reason themselves into stinginess and fear.
8.sharh: The courtesy of waiting might be mistaken for timidity. His father was quite capable of calculating a risk, and that same faculty made him more willing to run it or to give something away.

translation: God’s anger on Umm Dafr. Of all women
she is the likeliest to betray and lay waste.
9.sharh: He addresses the world by an old, ill-smelling nickname. Giving it a woman’s name allows the betrayal to sound personal before the second verb gives it the reach of time itself.

translation: A young woman, dark night her hair,
day her face, whose beauty the sun supplies.
10.sharh: Night and day furnish the young woman with dark hair and a luminous face. Her beauty looks permanently fresh because the two things that make it are renewed every evening and morning.

translation: The son of clay saw her already grey all over
with the Pleiades, the two Simaks and al-Wazn.
11.sharh: The same night that supplied a young woman’s hair is strewn with white stars. Adam, the human being made from clay, saw those marks of age at the beginning of human history.

translation: In those days she buried her daughter Eve.
How many generations she has buried in Eve’s wake.
12.sharh: He calls Eve the world’s daughter and uses the word for burying a daughter alive. Eve’s burial takes on new force when it becomes the first in a succession of whole generations.

translation: As though her children were born to her without
a husband, and she feared disgrace if she spared a son.
13.sharh: An unmarried mother who fears discovery might hide the fact that she has given birth. The world of the poem behaves as though even one surviving son could expose her.

translation: For all our eagerness we remain ignorant of what
is intended for us. Knowledge belongs to God, giver of favours.
14.sharh: The speaker joins the rest of humanity in its desire to know what is meant for it. Eagerness sharpens the question about the dead, but it gives the questioner no special access to an answer.

translation: Once a man is put out of sight, his story is secret.
Our thoughts bring back no news that will suffice.
15.sharh: Burial takes both a person and the means of finding out what has happened to him. Thought can keep sending enquiries after the dead, yet none returns with the news a son needs.

translation: Minds of the finest quality lose their bearings.
Even the strongest judgement is touched by weakness.
16.sharh: The word for these minds can describe pure gold or a person of penetrating judgement. If even minds of that quality lose their bearings, he can hardly expect certain news of the dead.

translation: Even the old masters of eloquence, whenever
they saw something exquisite, called it the work of jinn.
17.sharh: The finest speakers could praise an exquisite object by giving unseen artists the credit. Their turns of phrase survive, while the supposed workshop remains beyond anyone’s inspection.

translation: The world never kept anyone company for an hour
without proving deadlier than a matched opponent.
18.sharh: The studio gives “an hour” as a measure of time spent in the world’s company. Al-Tabrizi sees the hour itself as the companion that shortens a life. The words for keeping company and for an adversary share a root.

translation: We have learnt to relish the hurt this world gives us,
as if the miseries we gather were honey from the comb.
19.sharh: Bees have a harvest, and so do we. He gives honey and misery the same verb for gathering, making our appetite for a painful life sound as puzzling as a taste for bitterness in honey.

translation: No brown sandgrouse long for death. They travel
a five-day watering round, then drink foul water.
20.sharh: The sandgrouse spend their strength reaching a watering place. The promise of relief lasts almost to the rhyme, where the reward for the entire journey turns out to be stale water.

translation: They meet a falcon every day and night
and come to grief on its crooked talons.
21.sharh: The danger has a shape a reader can picture in the falcon’s hooked claw. Repeating the encounter across days and nights makes survival a continuing exertion for the birds.

translation: Nor do those restless through the night, who seem
from weariness and night travel like supple spears.
22.sharh: The commentators identify the new travellers as wild asses that approach water by night to avoid hunters. A long journey has reduced their bodies to the slender, flexible outlines of spear shafts.

translation: Four nights they beat a waterless waste with their hooves,
heading for water they cannot get a drop of.
23.sharh: The count is four nights this time, with hooves sounding on dry ground. The birds at least reached foul water. The wild asses cannot secure even the small measure for which they crossed the waste.

translation: Fear of death sheltered the sleepers in their cave
and set Noah and his son to building ships.
24.sharh: The young men taking refuge in the cave and the building of the ark are set beside the animals’ journeys. Fear becomes the agent of both sentences, finding shelter in one story and setting hands to work in the other.

translation: Even the souls of Moses and Adam found no sweetness in death,
though each had been promised a garden of Eden afterwards.
25.sharh: The preference for life reaches its strongest test in people promised a good abode after death. The verb asks what death tastes like to them, taking up the honey of the earlier verse.

translation: Master of rhymes, how often their obedience made
the eloquent Arabs seem tongue-tied foreigners to you.
26.sharh: The son addresses his father through a craft they shared. Rhymes obeyed him so readily that even accomplished speakers of Arabic might have seemed to be struggling with an unfamiliar tongue.

translation: May your new house bring you joy as you pillow
your right hand there in happiness and blessing.
27.sharh: A greeting for someone moving house is carried to a burial. The father rests upon his right hand, and the Arabic words for that hand and for good fortune sound as though the blessing already lies beside him.

translation: You live among neighbours far away
from the tribe. Rain on those homes and their people.
28.sharh: The dead have neighbours of their own, at a distance from the living encampment. A traveller’s familiar wish for rain upon a dwelling now falls on the graves and their inhabitants together.

translation: I went to Juhayna for certain news of them.
Juhayna, all you can give me is conjecture.
29.sharh: A proverb sends the enquirer to Juhayna for certain news. He takes the saying at its word and addresses Juhayna as someone close enough to hail by a shortened name. Even that informant can only hazard a guess about the dead.

translation: If you know me as someone who keeps asking,
I have had no true answer to put my mind at rest.
30.sharh: He imagines his informant recognising him as a persistent questioner. It is the quality of the answer that would end the enquiries. Simply hearing the same assurances again cannot do it.

translation: If excellence there has no advantage over failure,
what lasting misery, to be cheated so.
31.sharh: The conditional keeps hope and fear distinct. A man might have lived with care and generosity only to find no value placed on either. The loss sounds like the wrong done to someone cheated of his due.

translation: I pass the home you lived in as though
in reverence I were passing the Hijr and the Corner.
32.sharh: Two features of the Meccan sanctuary supply a measure for an ordinary street. The son’s passage by his father’s home has acquired the attentiveness of someone going past a holy place.

translation: Honouring your home is all my poor effort can manage.
Once the sword is lost, let dust cover the sheath.
33.sharh: His reverence for the building gives way to impatience with what he can still honour. An empty house has the value of an empty scabbard, and every gesture towards it recalls the blade it once contained.

translation: Your death has turned my heart into a bird
that swore it would never settle on a perch.
34.sharh: The heart undergoes a physical transformation before the bird is given a human power in return. It can take an oath, binding its own restless movements to the memory of the father.

translation: It spends what remains of its life with a wing
urged on, whether stopping or setting out.
35.sharh: The commentators picture a bird that begins to land and is at once driven to fly again. The opposing impulses keep the wing moving even at the instant that should bring it rest.

translation: Death’s call in your name was a snakebite
that tore my body, its venom blown into my ear.
36.sharh: The bite is inflicted through the ear. Death had only to speak a familiar name for a sound with no edge or substance to leave the son with the sensation of torn flesh.

translation: You groan, and my suffering at your groan follows of necessity,
as the accusative must follow inna.
37.sharh: The father’s groan suggests the sound of inna, a particle that puts its noun into the accusative. One Arabic word evokes both suffering and that grammatical case. The son’s suffering follows the sound as surely as the rule requires.

translation: You could not reach the morning, though night was passing,
like the lamp that burns out in the last watch.
38.sharh: Dawn is close enough to make the timing painful. The lamp has lasted through nearly the whole stretch for which it was needed, then uses up its remaining fuel before daylight.

translation: How many praise you as a matter of faith.
If only those who praise could turn death aside.
39.sharh: Words for praising a man and turning something aside nearly coincide in sound. Death would have many hands to deflect it if the likeness between the two acts extended beyond their names.

translation: Truth comes from the Lord on high to bring you
good news of favour, and Trust welcomes you with safety.
40.sharh: Truth and trustworthiness arrive as people to meet him, carrying the welcome he has earned. In Arabic the safety offered by Trust is audible in its very name.

translation: Another man’s witness speaks obliquely, from awe
and mercy. Question yours, and he need veil nothing.
41.sharh: The commentators understand the witness as the angel who testifies to a person’s deeds. A considerate witness might soften an embarrassing account. For his father, kindness and complete candour can go together.

translation: He will speak plainly of words more fragrant than musk
and deeds like the waters of Paradise, never stale.
42.sharh: The testimony appeals to smell and taste. The unspoilt water of his father’s conduct recalls, at a distance, the stale water to which the sandgrouse had to fly.

translation: A hand that did good, a man whose very breaths
were piety, and a tongue that never struck with words.
43.sharh: An unusual verb for doing someone a kindness grows from the noun “hand”. The tongue is equally capable of action, and its distinction here lies in the injury it never did.

translation: I wish you were laid beneath my eyelid, too noble
with qualities like those for my entrails or my side.
44.sharh: The word that meant a scabbard when he spoke of his father’s house now means his eyelid. Even the conventional wish to carry a loved one deep inside the body seems to him to offer too coarse a resting place.

translation: Even had they hollowed out a pearl, I could not
accept it for your body. I would spare it burial.
45.sharh: A pearl might seem a worthy answer to the search for a resting place. Hollow it out and it becomes another grave, and it is burial itself the son wants to spare his father.

translation: Had they lodged you in the open air, we would fear
its summer and winter, and cherish you more jealously still.
46.sharh: Space above ground brings its own exposures. The practical fear that his father might be too hot or too cold carries his old habit of looking after him beyond the point where it can help.

translation: Grave, how good your earth is when it lies soft
upon him. How those rough stones hurt.
47.sharh: Two nearly identical exclamations give the grave two entirely different voices. He approves of the soil to the extent that it cushions his father, then winces at the stones that might press on him.

translation: You have closed tight as an oyster. Keep safe
the pearl of honour that deserves your keeping.
48.sharh: Earlier he refused a pearl as a possible tomb. Here the pearl is his father, and the closing of the grave can be understood, for a moment, as the protective action of a shell.

translation: When I call to your grave, can you hear
your stricken son’s voice, your bondservant’s, I should say?
49.sharh: The son corrects his own name for their relationship as he speaks. Calling himself a bondservant is an act of deference, but neither form of address can establish whether the voice is heard.

translation: I shall weep when the ringdove’s young one sings for joy,
though what it means is the opposite of what I mean.
50.sharh: A dove’s call often sounds like lamentation in Arabic verse. He allows the bird its own intention, even delight. It is in passing from bird to listener that the song becomes an occasion for tears.

translation: Every singing girl sounds like a mourner in my ear,
however faultlessly she carries the tune.
51.sharh: One Arabic word means a melody and also an error in speech. The singer’s performance may be faultless in both respects, yet the mourner’s ear still converts her song into a funeral lament.

translation: I shall carry grief for you while I live. If I die
and meet you, I shall take no road back to grief.
52.sharh: Grief is something he has been carrying along a road. The condition that would release him is precise. Death would have to bring a meeting with his father, the person whose absence gave the burden its weight.

translation: After you, my heart desires no joy.
If it betrays you and courts delight, may it find none sweet.
53.sharh: Joy has become someone the heart might secretly court. The final wish turns on itself. If his heart breaks faith and seeks pleasure, he hopes the very thing it has sought will give it none.

1.1.5-6.head: ضاحِك المُزن
1.1.5-6.meaning: “The raincloud’s smile”, lightning flashing across a rain-bearing cloud.

1.2.2.head: جادَ
1.2.2.meaning: Poured rain generously on someone or somewhere.

1.2.6.head: الدَّجن
1.2.6.meaning: Darkness under a continuous cover of cloud.

2.1.4.meaning: Drew a sword from its sheath, here exposed the teeth in a smile. The same verb can also mean to sheathe.

2.2.3.head: النَّجلاء
2.2.3.meaning: Wide or gaping, said of the opening of a wound.

3.1.2.head: ثَنايا
3.1.2.meaning: The front teeth visible when someone begins to smile.

3.1.3.head: أَوانِس
3.1.3.meaning: Young women, here imagined as the teeth behind closed lips.

5.1.5.head: الكَرى
5.1.5.meaning: Sleep, including the dreams that come in sleep.

5.2.1-2.head: سُهد المُنى
5.2.1-2.meaning: “The wakefulness of wishes”, the desires that occupy the waking mind.

5.2.3.head: الجَيب
5.2.3.meaning: The opening of a garment at the breast, suggesting the thoughts kept within.

5.2.5.head: الرُّدن
5.2.5.meaning: A sleeve or the part of it close to the arm.

6.2.3.head: أُحُد
6.2.3.meaning: Uhud, a mountain near Medina. Its middle vowel is suppressed in this verse.

6.2.6.head: العِهن
6.2.6.meaning: Wool, especially dyed wool, to which mountains at the Resurrection are likened.

7.1.3.head: الحَوض
7.1.3.meaning: The Prophet’s pool, where people come to drink at the Resurrection.

7.1.4.head: الرَّوِيّ
7.1.4.meaning: Full enough of water to satisfy the thirsty.

7.2.6.head: اِستَأنى
7.2.6.meaning: Waited without hurrying, here letting others go first.

9.1.2-3.head: أُمّ دَفر
9.1.2-3.meaning: Umm Dafr, a disparaging name for the world, literally the mother of stench.

9.2.6.head: أَخنى
9.2.6.meaning: Laid waste to something, as time does to what people build.

10.1.1.head: كَعاب
10.1.1.meaning: A girl newly come to maturity.

10.1.3.head: فَرع
10.1.3.meaning: A full head of long hair.

11.1.2-3.head: سَليل الطّين
11.1.2-3.meaning: “The son of clay”, Adam, who in scripture was created from clay.

11.2.2.head: الثُّرَيّا
11.2.2.meaning: The Pleiades, a cluster of stars.

11.2.3.head: السِّماكان
11.2.3.meaning: The two Simaks, Arcturus and Spica in traditional Arabic star lore.

11.2.4.head: الوَزن
11.2.4.meaning: Al-Wazn, a southern star whose rising the commentators associate with that of Canopus.

12.1.3.head: وَأد
12.1.3.meaning: Burying a daughter alive, here extended to the world’s burial of its children.

12.1.4.head: حَوّاء
12.1.4.meaning: Eve, the mother of humankind, called the world’s daughter here.

16.1.3.head: الهِبرِزِيّ
16.1.3.meaning: Of the highest quality, here a mind of exceptional strength.

16.2.6.head: الأَفن
16.2.6.meaning: A failure of judgement or discernment.

17.2.6.head: الجِنّ
17.2.6.meaning: Jinn, beings normally unseen by humans and once credited with extraordinary craftsmanship.

18.2.7.head: قِرن
18.2.7.meaning: A matched adversary, especially in single combat.

20.1.5.head: كُدر
20.1.5.meaning: Brown or dusky sandgrouse, desert birds that fly to watering places.

20.2.2.head: الوِرد
20.2.2.meaning: The journey to water or the watering place itself.

20.2.3.head: خِمس
20.2.3.meaning: A five-day watering cycle in the traditional reckoning.

20.2.7.head: أَجن
20.2.7.meaning: Staleness in the taste or smell of water.

21.2.5.head: الحُجن
21.2.5.meaning: Hooked at the tip, of claws or talons.

22.1.2-3.head: قَلِقات اللَّيل
22.1.2-3.meaning: “The restless ones of the night”, wild asses travelling to water under cover of darkness.

22.2.2.head: الأَين
22.2.2.meaning: Exhaustion from exertion or a long journey.

22.2.5-6.head: القَنا اللُّدن
22.2.5-6.meaning: Supple spear shafts that bend without breaking.

23.1.2.head: مَليع
23.1.2.meaning: A long stretch of waterless country.

23.1.3.head: السَّنابِك
23.1.3.meaning: The tips or fronts of hooves.

23.2.7.head: مَعن
23.2.7.meaning: A meagre amount, here even a little water.

24.1.5-6.head: أَهل الكَهف
24.1.5-6.meaning: The Sleepers of the Cave, young believers who took refuge in a cave in Quran 18.

25.2.5-6.head: جَنَّتا عَدن
25.2.5-6.meaning: Two gardens of lasting abode, one promised to each of the two named prophets.

26.1.1-2.head: مَولى القَوافي
26.1.1-2.meaning: “Master of rhymes”, an address to the father as an accomplished poet.

26.2.5.head: اللُّكن
26.2.5.meaning: People who speak haltingly or with a foreign accent.

27.1.5.head: مُوَسِّد
27.1.5.meaning: Making something into a pillow or support.

27.2.4.head: اليُمن
27.2.4.meaning: Blessing or good fortune, echoing the word for the right hand.

28.1.2.head: سَكن
28.1.2.meaning: The inhabitants of a dwelling or settlement, here those who lie in the graves.

29.1.4.head: جُهَينَة
29.1.4.meaning: Juhayna, the tribe named in the proverb about where to find certain news.

31.2.6.head: الغَبن
31.2.6.meaning: Being cheated of one’s due or left at a disadvantage.

32.1.2.head: رَبع
32.1.2.meaning: A home or a place once occupied by a household.

32.2.4-5.head: الحِجر وَالرُّكن
32.2.4-5.meaning: The Hijr, the enclosure beside the Kaaba, and the Corner holding the Black Stone.

33.1.2.head: مَغنى
33.1.2.meaning: A dwelling once inhabited by its people.

33.2.4.head: العَفاء
33.2.4.meaning: Obliteration, or the dust that covers a trace.

34.2.5.head: وَكن
34.2.5.meaning: A bird’s resting place or perch.

35.2.5.head: الظَّعن
35.2.5.meaning: Departure from a dwelling or camp.

37.1.2.head: نَصب
37.1.2.meaning: Weariness or suffering, sounding like the grammatical term for the accusative.

37.2.6.head: إِنَّ
37.2.6.meaning: Inna, an emphatic particle whose subject takes the accusative.

38.2.6.head: الوَهن
38.2.6.meaning: A period of night, here its waning darkness.

39.2.3.head: حِمام
39.2.3.meaning: Death or the appointed end of life.

39.2.5.head: ثَنى
39.2.5.meaning: Turned something away from its course.

41.1.1.head: كَنى
41.1.1.meaning: Spoke indirectly or used a euphemism.

41.1.2.head: شَهيد
41.1.2.meaning: A witness to a person’s deeds, understood by the commentators as the attendant angel.

41.2.1.head: بُقيا
41.2.1.meaning: Consideration or mercy that leads one to spare someone.

43.1.2.head: يَدى
43.1.2.meaning: Did someone a kindness, from the Arabic word for a hand or a favour.

43.2.5.head: اللَّسن
43.2.5.meaning: Using the tongue to attack or disparage others.

44.1.3.head: جَفن
44.1.3.meaning: An eyelid, the same Arabic word as the scabbard in verse 33.

44.2.6.head: ضِبن
44.2.6.meaning: The side of the body beneath the armpit.

46.2.3.head: الضَّنين
46.2.3.meaning: Someone who guards a cherished person or possession jealously.

47.2.2.head: آهٍ
47.2.2.meaning: An exclamation of pain or regret.

47.2.4.head: جَنادِل
47.2.4.meaning: Large hard stones or pieces of rock.

48.1.3.head: المَحارَة
48.1.3.meaning: An oyster shell closing over a pearl.

49.1.5.head: رَمس
49.1.5.meaning: A grave or its low covering of earth.

49.2.6.head: القِنّ
49.2.6.meaning: A bondservant, especially one born into slavery.

50.1.4-5.head: اِبن وَرقاء
50.1.4-5.meaning: “Child of the grey dove”, a young dove.

51.1.1.head: نادِبَة
51.1.1.meaning: A woman who raises her voice in mourning for the dead.

51.1.5.head: قَينَة
51.1.5.meaning: A singing girl, traditionally an enslaved professional performer.

51.2.3.head: بَريّ
51.2.3.meaning: Free of fault. The poet uses the contracted form of the Arabic word for “free from”.

51.2.5.head: اللَّحن
51.2.5.meaning: A mistake in speech, especially in grammatical inflection.

53.2.7.head: هَنِئَ
53.2.7.meaning: May it give pleasure, here negated in a wish against his own heart.
